title: Which task fits a plain generative model?
scenario: You are using a general chatbot with no web access and no calculator tool. It generates responses from patterns learned in training.
task: Which of these requests is the best fit for that setup?

options.text: What is the current EUR/USD exchange rate, to four decimals?
options.feedback: Live rates change constantly and a plain model has no feed. It will produce a plausible number instead of the real one — and rarely admit the difference.

options.text: Compute the exact VAT on €8,432.19 at 21% and describe the legal rounding rule.
options.feedback: Two problems in one: language models are not reliable exact calculators, and the “legal rule” needs a verified source, not a prediction.

options.text: Turn these 14 messy meeting bullets into three clean paragraphs.
options.feedback: Yes — this is a transformation of text you supplied. Everything the task needs is inside your prompt, which is exactly where generative models are strong.

options.text: Give me the exact citation of a 2019 study, including page numbers.
options.feedback: Citations are a classic hallucination zone. A fluent-looking reference — authors, journal, pages — can be invented entirely, so this needs a real source.

hints: Ask: does the task need something the model cannot have — live data, exact computation, or verified sources?
explanation: Generative models shine at transforming content you provide: structuring, rewriting, summarizing, extracting. They are weakest exactly where you need guaranteed freshness, precision or provenance. Matching the task to the tool is the first practical AI skill — it prevents most “AI got it wrong” stories before they happen.
